title: Bakhoor and Incense: Scents of Arabia
summary: How families across Arabia burn fragrant wood chips called bakhoor, blended with precious resins like oud, to scent their homes and welcome guests.
poll: Old traditions like burning bakhoor matter less now that modern air fresheners exist.

versions.title: Bakhoor: Sweet Smoke of Arabia
versions.text:
Do you smell something sweet? A wood chip burns.

It is bakhoor. It has a rich scent.

Hot coals sit in a burner. Bakhoor goes on top. Smoke goes up. The scent fills the room.

The smoke can sit in your hair. It can sit in your clothes too.

Long ago, people burned bakhoor. They still do it now.

A rare wood is oud. It can make bakhoor smell rich.

Each home may mix bakhoor its own way.

A guest comes to the home. The host brings out the burner. It is a warm thing to do.

Bakhoor needs no spray can. It just needs wood, coals, and fire.

Bakhoor needs no spray can and no machine. It depends only on wood, coals, and fire to fill a home with scent.

versions.title: Bakhoor and Incense: Scents of Arabia
versions.text:
Imagine stepping into a home and noticing, within seconds, a warm aromatic scent filling the room, carried by bakhoor, a blend of wood chips and scented oils burned as part of a hospitality ritual across Arabia. Many visitors notice this rich scent, which seems to reach every corner of the house, before they even step through the door.

The method is simple, though the craft behind it is not. Chips of bakhoor are set atop glowing coals inside a small burner, often made of brass, silver, or clay, and as the wood warms, aromatic smoke rises and drifts through the room, settling into cloth and hair long after the coals cool.

Much of bakhoor's depth comes from resin, particularly oud, a dark and costly resin harvested from a rare tree that grows in only a handful of regions worldwide. Because good trees are difficult to find, this resin is gathered with great care and patience, and oud lends the rising smoke a warm, rounded note that many connoisseurs prize highly.

Crafting a fine bakhoor blend is the demanding work of trained artisans, not casual hobbyists experimenting at home. These artisans combine wood, resin, and oils in exact amounts, often guarding their recipe as a family secret that takes many years of patient practice to master.

This ritual reaches back further than most visitors to the region realize. For centuries, people throughout Arabia have burned aromatic wood and resin, both at home and as a mark of respect toward guests.

Hospitality remains at the heart of the custom even today. When visitors arrive, a host will carry the lit burner from room to room so everyone present can share in the rising scent.

Bakhoor also marks occasions worth remembering. During holidays and weddings, households often burn an unusually rich blend, treating the aromatic smoke almost as a form of celebration.

As part of the region's cultural heritage, bakhoor depends on nothing beyond wood, resin, and fire, and that simplicity helps explain why the ritual has endured across so many generations.
